Counter-Narratives

Military HistoryCounter-Narrative

The "Mad Mullah" Was Somalia's Greatest Scholar-Poet

"They called him mad. He composed 47 gabay of unmatched literary precision while waging war against three empires."

Winston Churchill labeled Sayyid Mohamed Abdullah Hassan the "Mad Mullah" in 1910. British newspapers repeated the epithet for two decades. What they didn't report: he held a doctorate in Islamic jurisprudence, spoke four languages fluently, and composed Somali classical poetry considered by scholars to be the finest gabay ever written — all while leading a 21-year military resistance that required the first aerial bombardment in African history to suppress.

The British Colonial Office files (declassified 1975) reveal internal memos expressing frustration at his strategic brilliance. One reads: "The Mullah is anything but mad — he has outmaneuvered our forces at every turn."

Spoken Heritage

Gabay — The Poetry That Shaped Nations

Before Somalia had written script, it had gabay — classical poetry so structurally complex that scholars compare it to Homeric epic. Each line follows strict alliterative rules, where every word must begin with the same sound. A master poet composes 80–100 lines entirely in their head, then recites without notes.

Gabay wasn't entertainment. It was how clans negotiated treaties, how leaders declared war, how history was preserved. A well-crafted gabay could prevent bloodshed or ignite conflict. The poet was diplomat, historian, and philosopher combined.
